SURGO × UNIVERSITY OF MANITOBA · CÔTE D’IVOIRE

Demand, services and modern contraceptive use

Women’s reported concerns are examined alongside the recorded facility environment in their own department and Rural/Urban area. Joint analysis helps identify places where service improvements, information and social support—or integrated responses—warrant investigation.

Initial evidence: higher personal demand scores are associated with lower modern use after adjustment. The selected supply-risk association remains uncertain. Geographic profiles identify relative concerns and service weaknesses; they do not establish causal binding constraints.

01 · DATA COVERAGE AND LINKAGE

Department–residence profiles attach local services to women

The source join retains 10,859 records: 10,856 have geographic identifiers, including 103 nonconsenting respondents; three records lack geography, weights and consent. The coverage map uses all geographically identified source records, before selecting women in need. Manitoba contains 3,078 facilities in 100 department-equivalent areas. Of 82 surveyed departments, 78 have both sources and four have women’s data only.

Dots show department facility counts, not actual facility coordinates. The 22 facility-only departments contain 366 records; 2,712 facility records contribute to the 78 linked departments. Seven display areas have neither source recorded. Boundaries use the CNTIG/OCHA archived 2018 layer, with Bonon, Gohitafla and Ouelle reconstructed from named subprefectures following official 30 September 2020 and 23 September 2020 decisions. These display updates conserve parent areas and do not change any woman/facility assignment.

How the assignment works

Woman’s recorded residenceAssigned supply environment
Department X · RuralAggregate the valid facility indicators among Rural facilities in Department X, then attach that profile to Rural women in Department X.
Department X · UrbanAggregate among Urban facilities in Department X, then attach that profile to Urban women in Department X.

Binary facility indicators become valid-response proportions; facility-level proportions become averages of valid facility proportions. Each facility contributes equally; there are no facility weights. This is aggregation before the woman-level join, not an average of profiles repeated across surveyed women. Facility residence is directly recorded in s1_5, rather than inferred from health-district type.

Unmatched areas: 153 women in Bonon, Facobly, Gohitafla and Taabo have no facility profile in the available crosswalk, including 49 women in need. Three additional source records have no geography. No Rural/Urban mismatch is repaired by borrowing another area, assigning zero or applying Senegal’s department fallback. These source gaps do not establish absence of services.

02 · USE, INTENTION AND METHOD CHOICE

Among women SURGO classifies as in need of family planning

Population from this section onward: original SURGO FPN2 = 1, unchanged, gives 4,292 women. No older script’s need_n recoding or sterilization/hysterectomy additions are applied. Women remain in overview results even when a model predictor is unresolved or a facility profile is unavailable.

Every bar and sub-bar uses all 4,292 women in need as its denominator. Percentages use WEIGHT; n is an unweighted respondent count. Capped whiskers are 95% logit intervals using the documented IDZD census-district clusters, constructed before need-domain selection. Original sampling strata and finite-population corrections are unavailable. Sub-bars overlap with current users and do not sum to 100%. 6 users have unresolved modern/traditional classification; 180 have another or unresolved initiation-preference response. *Preference concerns the wanted method at initiation; the alternative method type is not established. Future intention concerns any method, without a specified 12-month initiation window.

Initial pattern. Weighted current contraceptive use is 71.2%, including 57.0% confirmed modern use. Another 11.4% are nonusers with intention and 17.2% nonusers without stated intention. These are concurrent groups, not observed transitions from intention to adoption.

How the comparison methods work
ApproachScore constructionThreshold
Rank averageRank departments separately for each component, using average ranks for ties; average the six ranks.Demand above its final-score median; favorable supply below its median.
Mean percentagesAverage the six original percentages on each side.Same strict final-score median rule.
Median/IQRSubtract each component’s department median, divide by its IQR, then average six transformed values.Same strict final-score median rule.
Median countCount components above demand medians or below favorable supply medians.Flag at least four of six unfavorable comparisons.
Z-score average · primarySubtract each component’s department mean, divide by its sample SD, then average six component z-scores.Same strict final-score median rule.

Every continuous score requires six component summaries. Demand has 82 complete department scores; supply has 77. Component references use valid department values, with 78 departments for most supply components and 77 for free provision. Exact median ties are unflagged. No reduced-component score or outcome-informed threshold is substituted.

Five-method comparison ↓Exact thresholds ↓Component transformations ↓

Department planning profiles · z-score average

How the scores and thresholds are constructed
  1. Summarize the two sides by department. Demand is weighted valid-domain concern prevalence among women in need. Supply is unweighted facility summaries across all residence types.
  2. Standardize each component. Calculate (department value − mean of valid department values) ÷ sample SD. Departments contribute equally to this normalization reference; these are not survey weights.
  3. Average all six components. Higher demand means greater concern; higher raw supply readiness means stronger provision. The map uses department demand scores; models use each woman’s personal demand responses.
  4. Apply separate final-score medians. Flag demand strictly above -0.017469. Flag supply readiness strictly below -0.012715, equivalent to supply risk above 0.012715. Exact ties are unflagged.

Both flags → Both; one flag → Demand only or Supply only; no flags → Neither flagged. Missing supply gives Supply unassessed, rather than Demand only or Neither. These are relative planning profiles, not causal diagnoses or validated adequacy standards.

Both: 21Demand only: 18Supply only: 17Neither flagged: 21Supply unassessed: 5Facility data only: 22Neither source recorded: 7

Planning signal. The z-score approach flags 21 departments on both sides, 18 on demand only, 17 on supply only and 21 on neither. Supply is unassessed in five departments: four without facility profiles and Daoukro with undefined free provision. Use component evidence and local validation before selecting interventions.

Small samples: 61 departments have fewer than 50 women in need; 35 have fewer than 25. The smallest sample is 5. These exploratory estimates are retained with flags; rankings and classifications can be unstable. The 524 common-model exclusions are not applied to the map: each domain uses all available valid responses among women in need.

Planning priorities ↓All scores and classifications ↓
04 · ADJUSTED ASSOCIATIONS

Modern use in relation to personal concerns and local services

All models: 3,768 women with original SURGO FPN2 = 1, including 2,164 modern users across 77 departments. Outcome: current modern use = 1; confirmed traditional-only use or nonuse = 0. Adjust for age + age², Côte d’Ivoire-specific education, partnership, fertility goal and Rural/Urban residence. Use WEIGHT, department-clustered CR2/Satterthwaite intervals, and no random effects or interactions.

Score assigned to each womanConstructionObserved model variation
Demand risk scoreStandardize her own six demand responses using weighted item means and population SDs among valid FPN2 = 1 women; average all six. Her department or residence does not determine this score.62 distinct values across 3,768 women.
Supply risk scoreStandardize her assigned six exact department-residence measures against the valid department planning means/SDs. Average and reverse the sign: higher = weaker provision.121 distinct numeric scores across 121 department–residence contexts; No geographic fallback is applied.
ModelPredictors alongside the same covariates
1 · Demand scorePersonal demand score
2 · Supply scoreAssigned supply risk score
3 · Both scoresPersonal demand score + assigned supply risk score
4 · Six demand indicatorsEach woman’s six demand indicators separately
5 · Six indicators + supplySix personal demand indicators + assigned supply risk score

Key finding. In Model 3, the demand odds ratio is 0.37 (0.28–0.49) and the supply score odds ratio 0.92 (0.71–1.20) per one original average-z index point. The demand association remains after accounting for recorded supply and covariates. The supply interval includes 1, so its independent association remains uncertain. These do not allocate a percentage of nonuse to either side.

Planning interpretation. The curves show how predicted modern use varies with each score for the same women, holding other predictors at their observed values. Their levels and uncertainty are easier to interpret than odds ratios. They are adjusted cross-sectional comparisons, not expected gains from removing barriers. An uncertain supply slope does not establish adequate services.

Which reported concerns accompany lower use?

Models 4 and 5 retain personal responses separately. Model 5 also includes the same contextual supply score. The supply-only model is Model 2, shown again for reference.

Key finding. In Model 5, opposition to family planning has OR 0.16 (0.08–0.30); health beliefs have OR 0.66 (0.51–0.84); low method confidence has OR 0.67 (0.52–0.85). These individual intervals are pointwise. The six-indicator joint test has Holm p 0.705 with only 0.79 effective denominator degrees of freedom, so that block test is particularly weak. Use the heatmap to locate these concerns alongside service weaknesses; these associations do not establish which intervention would be most effective.

What this means for planning. The adjusted present-versus-absent difference is -39.8 percentage points for opposition and -8.6 points for health beliefs. The model predicts the same women under each response setting, retains their supply and other characteristics, and averages using WEIGHT. These gaps identify patterns to investigate; they are not intervention-effect estimates.

Unexpected direction. Healthcare permission barriers have OR 1.31 (1.06–1.60) and an adjusted difference of +5.4 points. This does not mean restrictions improve use: the item concerns general healthcare permission, and confounding, selection and reverse direction remain possible.

Each joint model has two tests. Demand tests its one score coefficient or all six concern coefficients together; supply tests its one score coefficient. Holm correction applies within those two tests per model. These tests do not establish whether demand matters more than supply, equality between them, or causal binding constraints.

DEFINITIONS, MISSINGNESS AND VERIFICATION

What the measures mean and what needs checking

Demand definitions and uncertainty
DomainSource and coding
Healthcare permission barriersHS7C: 1 = permission to see a doctor is a challenge; 2 = no. General healthcare permission, not FP-specific partner approval.
Anticipated social stigmaPB7B/C: 1/2 on either item about being seen or what others would say. Zero requires both valid 3/4 responses.
Health / side-effect beliefsPB2A–C: 1/2 on any item about health problems, reduced sexual desire or babies with birth defects. Zero requires all valid 3/4 responses. Bleeding and later fertility are excluded. Beliefs are not personally experienced side effects.
Future-fertility concernsMP4_a–f reversible-method concerns, requiring coherent MP4_a–i 0/1 selections, no none-plus-method contradiction, an explicit selection or none, and MP4_99 = 0. Sterilization items MP4_g/h do not create a concern.
Low method knowledge · retained labelMC5A/B: low confidence choosing a suitable method or handling side effects/switching (3/4 on either). This is confidence/self-efficacy, not objective knowledge. Zero requires both valid 1/2 answers.
Opposes family planningFP1: against (3/4) versus in favor (1/2). Unfamiliarity (5), no opinion (99) and other special responses remain unresolved.

A known positive establishes an any-concern flag even if another item is unknown. Zero requires valid negatives on every included item. Otherwise the domain remains unresolved. For health, raw 1/2 becomes concern, 3/4 becomes no concern and 99 remains unknown. These modules have responses among users and nonusers and are not restricted to married women.

PB2A alone has 30 unresolved responses (0.9% weighted), compared with 144 (3.8%) for the current PB2A–C composite. This report retains the broader definition; no PB2A-only model is substituted. Uncertainty is potentially informative, not necessarily a data error. Counts overlap across domains and the complete-case model may select more informed respondents.

Supply definitions and valid-response coverage
MeasureCalculation and interpretation
Short + long-acting offeringMean of UoM one_larc_3_sa_offer, joined as share_offer_larc_and_3_sa: share meeting the original ≥1 long-acting plus ≥3 short-acting product/category rule.
Free-product provisionMean of valid facility p_free_prod, joined as mean_p_free_prod. A value of 60% means the average reporting facility provides 60% of its recorded products free; not that 60% of facilities offer any free method.
Trained-provider shareMean of valid facility p_train proportions, using original UoM personnel/topic eligibility. Not the percentage of facilities with at least one trained provider.
FP counselor availabilitys7_2: Yes/(Yes+No); 1 = Yes, 2 = No, unknown/special responses excluded. Availability is not counseling receipt or quality.
At least one LARC in stockMean of one_larc_stockin, joined as share_stocked_1plus_larc. The country-wide three-LARC indicator is constant FALSE and cannot be standardized; this existing joined alternative is explicitly used.
Most-popular product in stockn_mp_in_stock_true/(true+false), among facilities with known status. Each facility refers to its own most-popular product, not the woman’s preferred method.

Apply these same facility definitions within department–residence cells for models and across all facilities in a department for planning. Facility aggregation is unweighted; missing responses are not automatically No. The source UoM definitions and their valid-response denominators are preserved.

Affected supply contexts and counts ↓
Original need flag, weights and available survey design

Original FPN2 = 1 identifies 4,292 women among 10,753 consenting positive-weight respondents, a weighted share of 40.8%. The original file records 6,461 as FPN2 = 0, 103 as 95 and three missing. No old researcher need_n or permanent-protection additions are used. All original source fields and rows are preserved.

Use final WEIGHT. The documented IDZD identifier is a unique census district/enumeration zone; 312 clusters are available among consenting weighted respondents, each nested within one department and residence type. Overview confidence intervals use that available cluster design, created before need-domain selection. Original sampling strata and FPC are not documented, so the full original complex design cannot be claimed. Department rates remain visible as weighted point estimates; logit intervals are not calculated where boundary proportions or zero design degrees of freedom prevent estimation.

All outcome models use modern use, retain WEIGHT, adjust for age + age², education, partnership, fertility goal and the woman’s Rural/Urban status. Primary uncertainty is department-clustered CR2 with coefficient-specific Satterthwaite intervals. Sampling-IDZD survey-GLM intervals are exported as a sensitivity; weighted point estimates agree. No random effects or interactions are fitted.

Low effective degrees of freedom and concentrated information

Abidjan accounts for 40.6% of the common model’s survey weight. Information is unevenly distributed across departments. Despite 77 nominal department clusters, the six-demand-coefficient joint HTZ test has only 0.79 effective denominator degrees of freedom. Its high p-value is not evidence that demand has no association. Pointwise coefficient intervals and the single demand-score test address different hypotheses and also have limited effective degrees of freedom.

Demand correlations use personal FPN2 = 1 responses and WEIGHT; supply correlations use one unweighted department profile. Correlated offering and stock features can receive overlapping weight in a six-component index. Equal weighting is explicit, not proof of equal intervention importance.

Independent verification passes 632 checks: every original survey field, all 1,278 department/context component values, all 65,154 individual assigned supply values including expected missingness, all ten weighted fits and CR2 covariance matrices, joint tests and PCA projections independently reproduced using weighted singular-value decomposition. Numerical correctness does not establish causal identification. The data are cross-sectional; attitudes can reflect contraceptive experience, and women can obtain care outside their assigned geographic environment.

APPENDIX · PCA SENSITIVITY

Alternative scores from the same personal and assigned service inputs

Separate weighted correlation PCAs use the same six personal demand indicators and six residence-specific supply measures among original FPN2 = 1 women. Demand PCA uses 3,954 complete women. Supply PCA uses 4,095 women with complete supply, equivalent to 121 profiles weighted by their represented women’s summed WEIGHT. These are not facility weights.

Supply PC1 is a contrast, not a general risk scale. Its coefficients are positive for offering, free provision, counseling and LARC stock, but negative for training and popular-product stock. The model uses its negative and labels it a Supply pattern score (PCA). Increasing it does not mean every supply condition worsens. The monotonic equal-weight z-score index remains primary.

What PCA retains. Demand PC1 captures 27.3% of variation in the demand inputs; supply PC1 captures 42.9% of the assigned supply variation. These are not percentages of modern use explained. The negative training/popular-stock coefficients must remain visible rather than being forced positive.

Final-weighted input means/population SDs and an eigendecomposition define the components. Each woman receives her personal demand projection and the projection of her exact department-residence supply values. PC1 is prespecified as a sensitivity. PC2 is reported but not entered into the current models; no PCA geographic classification is constructed.

Exploratory permutation and department-deletion checks describe construction stability, not formal survey-design tests. Supply PC1 does not exceed its exploratory permutation benchmark, reinforcing caution about a strong one-dimensional interpretation. The same 3,768 women enter all ten models. PCA units differ from average-z units, so odds-ratio magnitudes cannot be compared as measures of which approach or side matters more. Model intervals do not propagate score-estimation uncertainty.

The same five modern-use models using PCA scores

All models: 3,768 women with original SURGO FPN2 = 1, including 2,164 modern users across 77 departments. Outcome: current modern use = 1; confirmed traditional-only use or nonuse = 0. Adjust for age + age², Côte d’Ivoire-specific education, partnership, fertility goal and Rural/Urban residence. Use WEIGHT, department-clustered CR2/Satterthwaite intervals, and no random effects or interactions.

ModelPredictors alongside the same covariates
1 · Demand scorePersonal demand score
2 · Supply scoreAssigned supply risk score
3 · Both scoresPersonal demand score + assigned supply risk score
4 · Six demand indicatorsEach woman’s six demand indicators separately
5 · Six indicators + supplySix personal demand indicators + assigned supply risk score

Key finding. In Model 3, the demand odds ratio is 0.64 (0.58–0.71) and the supply score odds ratio 0.95 (0.87–1.04) per one oriented PC1 unit. The demand association remains after accounting for recorded supply and covariates. The supply interval includes 1, so its independent association remains uncertain. These do not allocate a percentage of nonuse to either side.

Planning interpretation. The curves show how predicted modern use varies with each score for the same women, holding other predictors at their observed values. Their levels and uncertainty are easier to interpret than odds ratios. They are adjusted cross-sectional comparisons, not expected gains from removing barriers. An uncertain supply slope does not establish adequate services.

Which reported concerns accompany lower use?

Models 4 and 5 retain personal responses separately. Model 5 also includes the same contextual supply score. The supply-only model is Model 2, shown again for reference.

Key finding. In Model 5, opposition to family planning has OR 0.16 (0.09–0.30); health beliefs have OR 0.66 (0.52–0.84); low method confidence has OR 0.67 (0.52–0.85). These individual intervals are pointwise. The six-indicator joint test has Holm p 0.424 with only 0.79 effective denominator degrees of freedom, so that block test is particularly weak. Use the heatmap to locate these concerns alongside service weaknesses; these associations do not establish which intervention would be most effective.

What this means for planning. The adjusted present-versus-absent difference is -39.6 percentage points for opposition and -8.7 points for health beliefs. The model predicts the same women under each response setting, retains their supply and other characteristics, and averages using WEIGHT. These gaps identify patterns to investigate; they are not intervention-effect estimates.

PCA interpretation. Supply PC1 has negative coefficients for trained-provider share and popular-product stock, alongside positive coefficients for other provision measures. Its negative is labeled a supply pattern score. It is not a monotonic supply-risk index, and its association cannot be interpreted as the effect of worsening every service domain.
